Bird flu has been confirmed in a backyard poultry flock in Rusk County, Wisconsin. Officials say all affected birds have been culled to prevent further spread.


## Bird Flu Confirmed in Northern Wisconsin


A new case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), commonly referred to as bird flu, has been confirmed in a backyard poultry flock in northern Wisconsin, raising renewed concerns about the spread of the virus among domestic and wild birds.


The Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection (DATCP) announced the detection on Thursday, November 12, identifying the affected flock in Rusk County, an area located north of Chippewa Falls.


According to state officials, the infected flock has been dealt with, and all affected birds have been culled to prevent the disease from spreading further. Authorities also confirmed that none of the birds will enter the commercial food supply.


The agency has not disclosed the exact location of the affected property. Officials have also not provided details explaining how the birds contracted the virus.


The latest detection highlights the continued challenges facing poultry owners and agricultural authorities as bird flu remains a concern across multiple parts of the United States.


## Officials Confirm Removal of Infected Birds


Following confirmation of the infection, authorities took action to eliminate the affected flock.


The DATCP stated that all birds from the infected backyard operation were culled. Their removal is intended to reduce the possibility of further transmission to nearby domestic poultry and other susceptible animals.


Officials emphasized that the birds would not be used for food production or enter the food supply.


Although the detection involves a backyard flock rather than a large commercial poultry operation, the case demonstrates that smaller poultry owners are also vulnerable to highly pathogenic avian influenza.


Backyard chickens and other domestic birds can come into contact with infected wild birds, contaminated surfaces, and materials that may carry the virus.


For this reason, agricultural authorities continue to encourage poultry owners to strengthen their biosecurity practices.


## What Is Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza?


Highly pathogenic avian influenza is a contagious viral disease that primarily affects birds. It is caused by certain influenza A viruses and can result in severe illness and significant mortality among infected poultry.


According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), avian influenza viruses are generally classified according to their ability to cause disease in birds.


Low pathogenic avian influenza strains typically cause milder symptoms. However, highly pathogenic strains can lead to severe disease and rapid deaths in affected poultry populations.


Common warning signs of highly pathogenic avian influenza include:


- Reduced energy levels and unusual behavior.
- Loss of appetite or reduced food consumption.
- Difficulty breathing or other respiratory symptoms.
- Swelling around the head, neck, or other body areas.
- Diarrhea and other digestive problems.
- Changes in egg production or abnormal eggs.
- Sudden or unexplained deaths among birds.


Poultry owners who notice these symptoms should avoid handling potentially infected birds and contact the appropriate agricultural authorities.


Early reporting can help officials investigate suspected infections and take measures to limit further transmission.


## How Does Bird Flu Spread Among Poultry?


Bird flu can spread through direct contact with infected birds or exposure to environments contaminated by the virus.


Wild birds are considered an important source of infection for domestic poultry. Chickens, turkeys, ducks, and other domestic birds may become infected after encountering infected wild birds or coming into contact with their droppings.


Transmission can also occur through contaminated equipment, clothing, footwear, and other materials.


People working around poultry operations can unintentionally carry the virus between locations if appropriate cleaning and disinfection procedures are not followed.


This makes biosecurity particularly important for backyard poultry owners, commercial farmers, and anyone who regularly handles birds.


## Wisconsin Officials Urge Poultry Owners to Strengthen Biosecurity


In response to the continued threat of avian influenza, Wisconsin agricultural officials are encouraging poultry owners to take preventive steps to protect their animals.


The DATCP recommends keeping domestic birds indoors whenever possible to reduce their exposure to wild birds and potentially contaminated environments.


The agency has also highlighted several important biosecurity measures that can help reduce the risk of infection.


These include washing hands thoroughly before and after handling animals, regularly cleaning and disinfecting equipment, and limiting access to poultry areas.


Owners should also avoid allowing unnecessary visitors into areas where birds are kept.


Another important precaution involves separating newly acquired birds from an existing flock or herd for at least 30 days. This isolation period can help identify potential infections before new animals are introduced to the rest of the population.


Consistent preventive practices are particularly important during periods when avian influenza activity is being reported.


## Bird Flu Continues to Affect Livestock Across the United States


The Wisconsin detection comes amid ongoing concerns about the spread of highly pathogenic avian influenza among animals nationwide.


Millions of poultry birds have been affected by bird flu outbreaks across the United States in 2026, according to the information provided in the original report.


The virus has also been detected in dairy cattle, expanding concerns beyond traditional poultry operations.


The USDA has reported infections in dairy herds across nearly two dozen states since the cattle outbreak began in March 2024.


States affected have included California, Idaho, Colorado, Texas, and Michigan.


More recently, federal authorities confirmed the first reported detection of bird flu in a dairy herd in Oregon. The announcement came only days after the virus was identified in cattle in Indiana.


In October 2026, two dairy herds in Washington also tested positive, marking the state's first confirmed cases of highly pathogenic avian influenza in livestock.


These developments demonstrate the importance of continued monitoring, testing, and cooperation between agricultural authorities and animal owners.


## Can Bird Flu Infect Humans?


Although avian influenza primarily affects birds, certain strains can occasionally infect other animals and humans.


According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 74 human cases of bird flu had been reported in the United States since 2024, including three deaths, as cited in the original report.


However, the CDC has maintained that the overall risk to the general public remains relatively low.


People who have frequent or direct contact with infected animals face a greater risk of exposure. This includes poultry farm employees, dairy workers, veterinarians, and others involved in handling potentially infected animals.


Individuals who work with birds or livestock should follow recommended protective measures, including wearing appropriate protective equipment and maintaining proper hygiene.


Avoiding direct contact with sick or dead wild birds is another important precaution.


People who believe they have been exposed to infected animals and subsequently develop symptoms should seek medical advice.


## What Happens Next?


The confirmation of bird flu in Rusk County serves as another reminder that avian influenza remains an ongoing concern for poultry owners and the wider agricultural industry.


While Wisconsin officials have confirmed that all birds in the affected backyard flock were culled, continued vigilance will be necessary to reduce the risk of additional infections.


Poultry owners are encouraged to monitor their birds closely, limit exposure to wild birds, maintain clean facilities, and report unusual illness or sudden deaths to agricultural authorities.


For now, officials have not released further information about the property involved or the suspected source of infection.


As bird flu detections continue across different animal populations in the United States, monitoring and preventive measures remain essential to protecting domestic poultry, livestock, and public health.
